exercise.name: Elbow to Knee Sit-up

reference.title: Elbow to Knee Sit-up
reference.listing: Page could not be read (gymvisual.com is blocked by the network proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice

equipment: Foot anchor (partner, strap or a fixed support)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl and sit up, inhale as you lower under control.
breathing.cadence: About 1.6 s up, a short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1.5 s up, brief pause, 2 s down; no jerking with the arms
prescription.progression: Slower lowering, then a pause at the knee, then a light plate on the chest

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat and anchored. Fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out, curl up and sit up, turning the trunk so the right elbow meets the left knee.
Breathe in and roll back down: low back first, head last.
Sit up again, turning the other way: left elbow to the right knee.
Roll down under control and keep alternating.

mistakes.mistake: Yanking the head with the hands to reach the knee
mistakes.fix: Fingertips only; turn the shoulder, not the neck.

mistakes.mistake: Twisting only at the top with a flat back
mistakes.fix: Curl first, then turn as you rise.
Lower for about 2 s, one vertebra at a time.

mistakes.mistake: Feet lifting or knees falling open
mistakes.fix: Anchor the feet and keep the knees hip width.

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: From lying to sitting most of the way up (clinical opinion)
Turn toward the opposite knee, mostly thoracic (clinical opinion)
Most of the second half of the rise is hip flexion (Andersson 1997)
About 90 degrees, feet anchored and still (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1.5 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Full sit-ups load the low back more than curl-ups: sit-ups gave higher compression than partial curl-ups in McGill's data (McGill 1998; Axler and McGill 1997).

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
The athlete mesh rests on the mat; the rig collision shapes are thicker than the mesh at the back and buttocks, so floorTolerance records how far those proxy shapes sink below the mat surface.
Loaded flexion with rotation is the combination most linked to disc stress in lab studies (Marshall and McGill 2010); keep reps moderate and skip it with disc symptoms.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest.
Low-back discomfort: stop at a three-quarter sit-up or a crunch.
Unanchored feet shift the work toward the abdominals (smaller range).
regressions: Sit-up with the hands reaching to the knees.
progressions: Light plate held on the chest.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the trunk off the mat and holds the pelvis as the hips flex: about 40% (upper) and 35% (lower) MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up (Escamilla 2016). In Konrad 2001 the sit-up kept rectus activity at the curl-up level while external oblique rose to about 57% MVC.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris take over once the shoulder blades are off the mat and pull the trunk up to the thighs. Flexed and supported (anchored) legs increased hip-flexor activation in hip-flexion sit-ups without changing abdominal activity (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris take over once the shoulder blades are off the mat and pull the trunk up to the thighs. Flexed and supported (anchored) legs increased hip-flexor activation in hip-flexion sit-ups without changing abdominal activity (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External oblique of the turning (elbow) side and internal oblique of the knee side rotate the trunk. Konrad 2001 found sit-ups already raise external oblique activity (about 57% MVC); the twist adds more (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External oblique of the turning (elbow) side and internal oblique of the knee side rotate the trunk. Konrad 2001 found sit-ups already raise external oblique activity (about 57% MVC); the twist adds more (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: about 23% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up versus 6% in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and it was higher in the traditional (hip-flexion) sit-up than in a trunk-flexion version (J Strength Cond Res 2015).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: about 23% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up versus 6% in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and it was higher in the traditional (hip-flexion) sit-up than in a trunk-flexion version (J Strength Cond Res 2015).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Keep the knees in line over the anchored feet (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Keep the knees in line over the anchored feet (clinical opinion).
